title: Why I Buy the Strongest Mining Stocks First — Not the Cheapest

keyPoints.text: Strategic investing in volatile mining stocks entails adding to positions step-by-step rather than taking binary all-or-nothing trades, functioning like an optimized version of dollar-cost averaging.

Gold mining stock selection focuses on technicals over fundamentals because gold has universal global demand regardless of production jurisdiction, whereas critical metals require domestic themes for market premiums.
Strategic dollar-cost averaging involves building positions across individual stocks and the broader portfolio rather than attempting to achieve a perfect market entry.

Technically strong mining stocks tend to attract institutional trend-following capital first, whereas technically weaker stocks typically decline much harder during sector pullbacks, creating opportunistic entry points if market corrections occur.

Prioritizing strong, leading mining stocks first mirrors institutional behavior, while weaker mining stocks can be accumulated later at discounted prices during market corrections to lower overall portfolio entry averages.
An upcoming shift in the mining industry will require adjustments to the accumulation strategy for mining stocks.
